newsitem.title: UK: Polls suggest UK Labour heading for landslide win.
newsitem.headline: Polls suggest UK Labour heading for landslide win.

text.p: Britain's revamped Labour Party appeared poised to end 18 years in opposition with a landslide victory in the May 1 national election on a scale unseen since the end of World war Two.

Four opinion polls in Sunday newspapers said Labour was leading the ruling Conservatives by between 15 and 24 percentage points, a lead which could translate into a parliamentary majority of up to 200 seats.

Several newspapers threw caution to the winds in predicting that in five days time Labour leader Tony Blair, who has ditched much of the party's old socialist dogma, would become Britain's youngest prime minister this century.
"Starting this week; a new era" said the front page of the Observer.
"Labour landslide" said the Independent on Sunday, adding that many Conservatives were privately convinced that Prime Minister John Major had lost his uphill battle to retain power.
Even before the votes were cast, one outspoken Conservative, Edwina Currie, hit out at campaign style of her party and predicted a bloodbath among the leadership.
"The whole style of the campaign is wrong," she wrote in the staunchly Conservative Sunday Express. "Tony Blair has not just talked about being tough, he has done it..."
Currie forecast that Labour would get a majority of 100, possibly rising to 150-180, and added: "After May 1 there will be a bloodbath in the Tory (Conservative) party."

Blair, 43, has moved Labour sharply to the right to attract crucial middle class votes, pledging not to raise income tax for five years and embracing previously despised Conservative policies on privatising state industries.
"I want a country that is not divided by class. We will try to restore honour and decency," he told supporters on Saturday.

Major, battling internal divisions over the European Union and a string of sleaze scandals within his party, has been unable to capitalise on a booming economy of low inflation and falling unemployment.
Labour got an unexpected boost when Britain's biggest-selling Sunday newspaper, The News of the World, threw its weight behind the "time for change" sentiment voiced by many Britons.
"We back Blair, the man for the new millennium" it declared.
The influential Sunday Times decided, with some reluctance, to maintain its backing for the Conservatives, saying that newly-reformed Labour could not be fully trusted.

"The electorate should not kid itself that a vote for Labour is a vote for safe change, however seductive the message from Mr Blair. Only the Tories, warts and all, offer the prospect of lasting improvement," it said.
Other heavyweight Sunday newspapers, including the Telegraph and the Mail, urged their readers to give the Conservatives another chance.
Major sought to woo the estimated 20 percent of voters who are still undecided, saying jobs, mortgages and savings would all be put at risk under a Labour government.
"So is it time for a change?" Major asked at a news conference. "Your life would change under Labour, but it would change for the worse and some of that change would be irreversible."
